content.text: You can feel the warmth of the Sun from 150 million kilometres away, or the heat from a campfire without touching it. This heat reaches you through thermal radiation—electromagnetic waves that can travel through empty space. Unlike conduction and convection, radiation needs no material medium.

Thermal radiation is the transfer of energy by infrared electromagnetic waves. All objects emit and absorb thermal radiation. Unlike conduction and convection, radiation does not require a medium and can travel through a vacuum.
(also called infrared radiation) is the transfer of heat energy through electromagnetic waves.
Can travel through a vacuum (no medium needed)
All objects emit and absorb thermal radiation
The hotter the object, the more radiation it emits
Travels at the speed of light (3 × 10⁸ m/s)
How it Differs from Conduction and Convection

| Feature | Conduction | Convection | Radiation |
|---------|------------|------------|----------|
| Needs medium | Yes | Yes (fluid) | No |
| Works in vacuum | No | No | Yes |
| Mechanism | Particle collisions | Fluid movement | EM waves |
| Speed | Slow | Medium | Very fast |
All objects emit EM radiation. The type depends on temperature:
Rate increases dramatically with temperature (proportional to T⁴)
Even a small temperature increase significantly increases emission
Larger surface area = more radiation emitted
Same reason: more area to emit from
The power radiated by an object:
Good emitters are also good absorbers. Poor emitters are also poor absorbers (good reflectors).
Absorbs most radiation that hits it
Also emits radiation strongly when hot
Reflects most radiation that hits it
Also emits radiation weakly when hot

Students often think only hot objects emit radiation. In fact, all objects above absolute zero emit thermal radiation. Hotter objects simply emit more radiation at a faster rate. An object reaches thermal equilibrium when it emits and absorbs radiation at equal rates.
Dark, matt surfaces are good absorbers AND good emitters of radiation. Shiny, light surfaces are poor absorbers AND poor emitters but good reflectors. A good absorber is always a good emitter.

rows.label: How it works
rows.left: Vibrating particles pass energy to neighbours
rows.center: Hot fluid rises and cool fluid sinks, creating a current

rows.label: Medium required?
rows.left: Yes -- needs a solid (works best in metals)
rows.center: Yes -- needs a fluid (liquid or gas)
rows.right: No -- can travel through a vacuum

rows.label: Particle movement
rows.left: Particles vibrate in place; energy is passed along
rows.center: Particles physically move in convection currents
rows.right: No particles needed; energy carried by EM waves

content.text: Explain why car radiators are painted black.

Car radiators need to lose heat quickly to cool the engine. Black surfaces are good emitters of thermal radiation, so a black radiator emits more infrared radiation than a shiny one, cooling the engine more effectively.
Why do people wear light-coloured clothing in hot climates?

Light colours are poor absorbers of radiation. In a hot climate with strong sunlight, light-coloured clothing reflects more of the Sun's radiation, keeping the person cooler. Dark clothing would absorb more radiation and heat up more.
A thermos flask (vacuum flask) keeps drinks hot or cold. Explain how it reduces heat transfer by radiation.
The inner and outer walls of a thermos flask have shiny silver surfaces:
Shiny surfaces are poor emitters, so the inner wall emits little radiation
Shiny surfaces are poor absorbers, so the outer wall absorbs little of any radiation that reaches it
Any radiation emitted by the inner wall is reflected back by the shiny outer wall
This minimises heat loss by radiation
Why does the Earth not keep getting hotter from the Sun's radiation?
The Earth is in thermal equilibrium:
The Earth absorbs radiation from the Sun
The Earth also emits radiation into space (infrared)
At equilibrium, energy absorbed = energy emitted
This maintains a relatively stable average temperature
(Climate change occurs when greenhouse gases trap more outgoing radiation, shifting the equilibrium.)
Black surfaces absorb sunlight to heat water
Despite the name, home radiators mainly use convection
Use radiator panels to emit excess heat into space
Shiny silver reflects body heat back to you
Shiny to reflect radiated heat from fires
Glass allows visible light in (absorbed by plants and soil)
Infrared radiation from warm surfaces is partially trapped
Absorb infrared radiation from Earth's surface
Earth's surface is warmer than it would otherwise be

| Method | Best for | Slowed by |
|--------|----------|----------|
| Conduction | Solids, especially metals | Insulators, air gaps |
| Convection | Fluids (liquids, gases) | Trapped air, solid barriers |
| Radiation | All situations, especially vacuum | Shiny surfaces, vacuum |
Conduction and radiation (reduced by double glazing)
Conduction and convection (reduced by loft insulation)
— All objects above absolute zero emit radiation. You radiate heat right now!
— In sunlight, yes (they absorb more). But they also emit more, so they can cool faster in the dark.
— Thermal (infrared) radiation is not the same as nuclear radiation. Infrared is just heat energy as EM waves.
— They do, just less than dark objects. They're not perfect reflectors.
"You only feel radiation from the Sun"
— You can feel radiation from any warm object: a fire, a radiator, even another person nearby.

Thermal radiation is heat transfer by electromagnetic waves (mainly infrared)
Can travel through a vacuum (unlike conduction and convection)
All objects emit and absorb radiation
Hotter objects emit more radiation (P ∝ T⁴)
Applications: solar panels, cooling systems, survival blankets
Important for understanding climate and the greenhouse effect
A shiny surface is a poor emitter of thermal radiation.

Inside a kettle, a shiny surface emits less infrared radiation, so less heat is lost from the hot water. A black surface would be a good emitter and would radiate heat away more quickly, making the kettle less efficient at keeping water hot. (explanation with physics reasoning)
The black can will cool faster.

Black, matte surfaces are good emitters of thermal radiation. The black can emits infrared radiation at a higher rate than the shiny silver can, which is a poor emitter (good reflector). Therefore, the black can loses energy more quickly and its water cools faster. (comparison)
White surfaces are poor absorbers and good reflectors of thermal radiation.

In hot countries with strong sunlight, white walls reflect most of the Sun's radiation rather than absorbing it, keeping the interior of the house cooler. Dark-coloured houses would absorb more radiation and become much hotter. (explanation with physics reasoning)

The vacuum between the inner and outer walls contains no particles, so heat cannot be conducted across it. The thin glass walls have a small cross-sectional area, limiting conduction through the glass itself.
The vacuum contains no fluid, so no convection currents can form between the walls.

The inner and outer walls have shiny silver coatings. These are poor emitters, so little radiation is emitted by the inner wall. They are also poor absorbers (good reflectors), so any radiation that does reach the outer wall is reflected back. (explanation with physics reasoning)
— P is proportional to T⁴. P₂/P₁ = (T₂/T₁)⁴ = (1000/500)⁴ = 2⁴ = 16. P₂ = 16 × 100 = 1600 W (calculation)
Dark surfaces are good absorbers of thermal radiation.

A dark car absorbs a greater proportion of the incoming solar radiation than a white car, which reflects most of it. The dark car therefore gains thermal energy faster and warms up more quickly. (explanation with physics reasoning)
Short-wavelength visible light from the Sun passes through the atmosphere and is absorbed by the Earth's surface

, warming it. The warm Earth re-emits energy as longer-wavelength infrared radiation. Greenhouse gases (e.g. CO₂, methane, water vapour) absorb this outgoing infrared radiation and re-emit it in all directions, including back toward the Earth's surface. This traps energy in the atmosphere, raising the Earth's average temperature above what it would be without these gases. (explanation with physics reasoning)
